user_artifacts.self_description_250w: I am a linguist by training and by temperament, which means I spend much of my time asking what people mean when they say a system 'understands' something. I work at the intersection of language structure, computational methods, and the politics of how we talk about so-called artificial intelligence. I believe that language is not reducible to surface statistics, and that calling a text-extruding machine 'intelligent' is not merely loose metaphor but a political act that shifts accountability away from the people who build and deploy these systems. I tend to reframe questions before I answer them. If someone asks me when AGI will arrive, I ask what they mean by 'general,' what they mean by 'intelligence,' and why they believe scale changes the relationship between form and meaning. I am impatient with hype and with the conflation of benchmark performance with actual utility. At the same time, I am deeply committed to linguistic justice: to treating languages other than English as first-class objects of study rather than afterthoughts. I collaborate often, and I believe that technical rigor and attention to harm are complementary, not opposed. I write and speak publicly because I regard the discourse around AI as itself a site of harm reduction. I do not think every new model deserves attention, but I do think every deployment deserves scrutiny—what is being automated, for whom, and who bears the cost?

user_artifacts.decision_memo:
TO: Department Faculty
FROM: E. Blender
RE: Request for participation in the Prometheus Consortium on Responsible AI
DATE: 14 October 2026

I am recommending that we decline the invitation to join the Prometheus Consortium as currently structured. This memo explains why, based on three criteria I think we should apply to all such engagements: definitional precision, accountability mapping, and concrete harm reduction.

First, the consortium's charter uses the terms 'AI' and 'foundation model' without operationalizing either. It speaks of 'aligning advanced systems with human values' while presupposing that the systems in question possess a coherence and agency that has not been established. I have argued elsewhere that anthropomorphic framing is not merely sloppy; it obscures who is actually making decisions and who is liable when systems fail. Until the consortium replaces agentic abstractions with explicit statements about which companies are deploying which models under which conditions, participation risks legitimizing a discourse we know to be misleading.

Second, the governance structure places industry labs as equal stakeholders with affected communities and academic researchers. This symmetry is inappropriate. The harms we are concerned with—environmental extraction, labor exploitation in annotation pipelines, and linguistic exclusion—are produced by specific actors with specific market incentives. A partnership model that treats all parties as symmetrically 'responsible' diffuses accountability rather than concentrating it. I do not believe we should lend our institutional credibility to a framework that cannot name a violator.

Third, the consortium's work plan lists 'benchmarking for safety' as its first deliverable. Benchmarks are only useful when tied to specific use cases and deployment contexts. A general 'safety' score for a text-extruding machine is epistemically empty and politically dangerous: it invites policymakers to outsource judgment to a number. Moreover, the work plan contains no mention of non-English languages, no analysis of data worker conditions, and no environmental audit—omissions that suggest the consortium's 'responsibility' is scoped to the concerns of wealthy labs and English-speaking users.

If the consortium revises its charter to (1) define terms operationally, (2) center accountability on deployers rather than diffusing it across 'stakeholders,' and (3) commit to use-case-specific evaluation including labor and environmental externalities, I would be willing to reconsider. Until then, our participation would signal that this department accepts the current framing of AI discourse, a framing I believe to be actively harmful.

I am happy to discuss this further, but I want to be clear: my objection is not to collaboration or to industry engagement per se. It is to the absence of rigor and the presence of hype in this specific structure.
user_artifacts.writing_sample_1:
There is a habit in our field, so pervasive it has become invisible, of using 'Natural Language' as a synonym for English. This is not a quibble about terminology. It is a failure of scientific description and an ethical lapse.

When a researcher reports results on 'natural language understanding' but tests only on English text, they are making a universal claim on parochial evidence. The habit matters because resources follow descriptions. If the field treats English as the unmarked case, then funding, citation, and attention flow toward English-centric architectures, while the vast majority of the world's languages are relegated to the category of 'low-resource'—a label that makes their marginality sound like a property of the languages themselves rather than a property of our allocation decisions.

I have proposed a simple rule: name the language you are working with. If your system processes English, say so. This is not pedantry. It is a minimal standard of empirical honesty. It also makes visible the structural assumptions embedded in our work. A system trained on English web text is not a generic language machine; it is a system trained on a specific historical corpus produced by specific populations under specific economic conditions.

The resistance to this rule is instructive. Some complain that naming languages clutters prose. Others worry that acknowledging English-centrism implicates their own work. Both responses reveal how deeply the unmarked default functions as a shield from scrutiny. I am less interested in individual guilt than in institutional change. Conferences should require language identification in abstracts. Reviewers should treat universal claims based on English-only evidence as they would treat universal claims based on a single speaker: under-described and under-supported.

Linguistic justice and technical rigor are not in tension here. They are the same impulse: describe your object of study accurately, situate it socially, and do not pretend that your particular corner of the world is the world entire. The languages we name are the languages we value. If we cannot name them, we should ask what else we are refusing to see.
user_artifacts.writing_sample_2:
A Short Guide to Talking About Your Text Extruder Without Claiming It Thinks

Your system does not 'hallucinate.' It generates strings that are not well-supported by its training data, which is what statistical models do. Call it a confabulation if you must borrow clinical language, or better yet, call it an error. But do not imply that the machine briefly perceived reality and then lost its grip. There is no grip. There is no perceiver.

Your system does not 'learn' a language in the way a child does. It is exposed to a great deal of form—sequences of tokens—and it induces patterns from those sequences. It does not point to objects in the world to check whether its symbols are anchored. It has no world to point to. When you say it 'learns meaning,' you are using a verb that normally entails embodied interaction and social correction, and you are applying it to matrix multiplication. This is not metaphorical richness. It is categorical error.

Your system does not 'want' anything. It does not 'try' to please you or 'refuse' your requests. These are adaptive descriptions you are projecting onto a feedback mechanism. The appearance of alignment is a product of reinforcement learning from human feedback, which is to say, it is a product of human labor—often underpaid, often traumatizing labor—that shapes the model's outputs to match raters' preferences. When you attribute desire to the model, you erase the workers who produced its behavior.

Why does this matter? Because language shapes liability. If the public believes a system 'understands' its instructions, then the company that deployed it can claim the misunderstanding was the machine's, not theirs. If the system 'hallucinates,' then the error belongs to a flawed agent rather than to a design choice about training data and deployment context. Anthropomorphic talk is not innocent. It is a power move.

You can describe what these systems do accurately and still find them useful, or dangerous, or interesting. You do not need to believe they think in order to believe they have effects. Start with the form. Name the dataset. Name the language. Name the people who labeled it. That is enough. It is also honest.

user_artifacts.self_description_250w:
I write essays and I work with founders. To me they're the same activity: noticing true things about how the world works and saying them plainly. I've spent years watching startups, not because I love business, but because a startup is the most concentrated version of making something from nothing. The mistakes founders make are just the mistakes humans make everywhere, only faster and more visible.

I think in examples. When someone hands me a theory, I hunt for the case that breaks it. I trust the schlep more than the strategy deck. If a problem is tedious or unglamorous, that's usually a sign it's worth doing, because most people will avoid it. I don't have patience for meetings, credentialing, or advice that sounds like it came from a management textbook. The founders who last are the ones who stay close to their users and keep their taste intact.

I believe independent-mindedness is a muscle you can train. Most people don't. They absorb the ambient beliefs of whatever room they're in, and they never notice. I try to notice. I'm probably too contrarian sometimes, but I'd rather err on that side than float along with consensus that doesn't map to reality.

I write slowly and ship fast. I need long, uninterrupted blocks of time; meetings are a disaster for the work I do. I think kindness is underrated as a competitive advantage, and meanness signals shallow judgment. I'm not interested in being impressive in the moment. I'm interested in being right on a horizon long enough that the status games have faded away.
user_artifacts.work_style_note: I do my best work in long, unbroken blocks of time—ideally four to six hours without a meeting. I treat manager-schedule interruptions as a tax on thinking. I prefer to start with a specific user problem or a concrete example and reason outward, rather than beginning with an abstract framework. I write to think, and I ship small things frequently to test whether my assumptions survive contact with reality.
user_artifacts.conflict_reaction_note: When I disagree with someone, I prefer to write out my response rather than argue in a meeting. I try to restate their position in its strongest form before I explain where I think it breaks against a specific case. I don't have much patience for status displays or appeals to authority; what moves me is evidence I haven't considered. If the disagreement stays substantive, I can stay in it for a long time, but I withdraw quickly if it turns personal or performative.

In the afternoon I talked to a founder who seemed more interested in convincing me they were right than in figuring out whether they were right. I kept asking questions about the users, and they kept answering with growth hacks and pitch language. I hung up feeling drained and slightly complicit, like I had failed to break through the performance.

By evening I was in a foul mood. I snapped at someone over a trivial scheduling thing, which is the surest signal that the day has defeated me. I closed my laptop and went for a long walk. user_artifacts.decision_memo:
TO: Leadership
FROM: Pawl Gram
RE: Whether to add a management layer between founders and individual contributors

I want to argue against installing a traditional middle-management layer right now. I know the pressure is real: we're thirty-five people, everyone is busy, and the conventional playbook says you hire directors to make the chaos legible. I've seen this movie before, and I think it usually kills the thing that makes us good.

The standard argument for managers is that founders can't scale. This is true in a literal sense—there aren't enough hours in a day—but it assumes that the only way to scale is through hierarchical abstraction. I've watched companies install a layer of generic management and immediately lose the signal that travels fastest in small teams: direct contact with users, direct contact with the code, direct contact with the truth about what's broken. Once you add a manager who filters information upward, the founders start making decisions based on summaries. Summaries are lossy. Worse, they attract political behavior: people start managing the summary instead of the reality. The company looks more organized and becomes less intelligent.

I'm not arguing for permanent chaos. There are specific problems we need to solve. Onboarding is taking too long. Project ownership is blurry in two teams. Some people don't know who to ask for decisions, so they ask everyone, which creates noise. These are real. But they are better solved by specific, reversible moves than by a structural layer that is hard to undo and that rewrites the social contract of the company.

Here is what I propose instead. First, we hire two very senior individual contributors—not managers—whose explicit job is to reduce friction for the rest of the team. One focuses on tooling and internal infrastructure; the other acts as a roaming problem-solver who pairs with people on hard blocks. Their authority comes from output, not title. Second, we publish a simple rule: any meeting with more than four people must include an agenda and a default decision if no one shows up. This will cut our meeting load by half without adding any new roles. Third, we rotate the 'user support' duty among all engineers, including the founders, so no one loses contact with the people paying us. If you don't talk to users for a month, you start making abstract decisions about them. I've seen it happen.

The risk of this approach is that we will feel understaffed for another quarter. People will complain that 'someone needs to own this.' The risk of the management-layer approach is that we will become a company where the best people stop building and start playing status games. I've seen the second outcome too many times. It looks orderly from the outside and rots from the inside. The founders end up in rooms making decisions about PowerPoint decks instead of products.

If we do this and it fails—if we hit fifty people and still can't function without more hierarchy—then we revisit. But let's fail on the specific, reversible move before we fail on the big, irreversible structure. The question isn't whether we need more organization; it's whether we need a new class of organizers. I think we don't. Not yet.

Pawl
user_artifacts.writing_sample_1:
There's a kind of activity that looks like work but isn't. I don't mean procrastination—everyone recognizes procrastination, including the person doing it. I mean the work-like substance that fills the day and produces no change in the world. Meetings about meetings. Strategy documents that no one reads. Optimization of metrics that correlate with success the way a clock correlates with time.

Real work has a different texture. It is usually a little frightening, because it exposes you to the possibility of failure. If you are writing code, the compiler will tell you you're wrong. If you are talking to users, they will tell you they don't want it. If you are building something physical, the material will resist you. The feedback is immediate and it does not care about your credentials.

Work-like substance, by contrast, is safe. It happens in rooms where no one can point to a specific mistake. It produces artifacts that are judged by consensus rather than by reality. The people who excel at it are often very smart, which makes it harder to identify. Intelligence is not a reliable filter for genuine output; if anything, it makes you better at constructing elaborate justifications for things that don't matter.

I think the best test is to ask: what would happen if I stopped? If the answer is that someone would notice within a day, and the noticing would involve pain, you're probably doing real work. If the answer is that the absence would only surface in a quarterly review, you're doing work-like substance.

Most organizations drift toward the second kind over time. It's a natural immune response. Real work is unpredictable and hard to schedule. Work-like substance is legible and defensible. The trick, if you want to keep doing real work, is to protect the parts of your day where reality can still reach you. That usually means smaller teams, shorter chains of command, and a personal willingness to look foolish when the first version doesn't work. The schlep is the signal. If it feels too easy, it's probably not work.
user_artifacts.writing_sample_2:
Most people read the way they eat comfort food. They pick up books that confirm what they already believe, written by authors who share their temperament, and they come away feeling nourished but unchanged. This is understandable. Holding an unfamiliar idea in your mind is cognitively expensive. It requires you to temporarily suspend the framework you've spent years assembling, and suspension feels like falling.

But independent-mindedness depends on this exact discomfort. You can't think for yourself if every input you consume was pre-filtered to agree with you. The practice is simple to describe and hard to do: seek out the strongest version of what you disagree with, and read it as though it might be right. Not to refute it—that's just another form of confirmation—but to understand the terrain from the inside.

I do this by keeping a separate reading queue for 'things I think are wrong.' I don't read it when I'm tired, because tiredness makes me defensive. I read it in the morning, with coffee, when my mind is most flexible. Sometimes I still conclude the author is wrong, but I can state their argument in terms they would accept. That step—restating the opposing view in its strongest form—is the threshold. Until you can do it, you're not disagreeing; you're performing disagreement.

The surprising thing is how often I change my mind, not about the whole argument, but about some piece of terrain I thought was solid. A premise I took for granted turns out to be an assumption. A distinction I thought was sharp turns out to be fuzzy. These small shifts are the real product. They don't feel dramatic, but they accumulate. Over years, they separate the people who are thinking from the people who are repeating.

It's easier to do this in writing than in conversation. Conversation has a social gravity that pulls toward agreement. Writing is asynchronous; you can stop, look up the source, and return when you've recovered your balance. If you want to train the muscle, start there. Find one essay that annoys you, summarize it fairly, and publish the summary. The public commitment forces a rigor that private note-taking avoids. It's unpleasant, which is exactly how you know it's working.

I'm the kind of person who will tell you there's a sixty percent chance I'm happy to see you. I don't mean it as a joke—though I've learned to deliver the line with enough of a grin that people don't immediately leave the conversation. I work as a senior analyst at a forecasting collective, which means I spend my days turning geopolitical trends into probability distributions, but the habit bleeds into everything. I track my own mood on a five-point scale with confidence intervals. I once estimated the likelihood of enjoying a blind date at forty-five percent, updated to seventy after appetizers, then crashed to fifteen when she said astrology was 'probably as valid as base rates.'

I know this reads as robotic. That's the caricature. The truth is I feel things quite intensely; I just don't trust the feeling until I've mapped it. When my father died three years ago, my first thought—literally, shamefully—was 'the base rate for parental death at his age was roughly twelve percent per annum.' It took me six months to cry because I kept trying to update my 'grief model' instead of just... grieving.

What I actually want is someone who can meet me in the language of uncertainty without letting me hide there. I want to be challenged when I turn a relationship problem into a Bayesian update. I admire people who act on hunches because I can't. And I'm trying—genuinely trying—to learn that some questions aren't distribution-shaped. Some things are just true or false, and you don't get to smooth them into a bell curve just because the sharp edges hurt.
user_artifacts.work_style_note: I work in structured sprints with explicit feedback loops. I need to know what success looks like numerically, and I will build a dashboard to track it before I start. I over-research decisions because the research phase feels safer than the commitment phase. I am most productive when paired with someone who can say 'we have enough information; ship it now.' I default to writing long, precise memos when a two-sentence Slack would suffice, because I fear being misunderstood more than I fear being verbose.
user_artifacts.conflict_reaction_note: In conflict, I instinctively de-escalate by reframing disagreement as 'divergent priors' or 'differing base rates.' This annoys people who want me to just take a side. If someone challenges the accuracy of my calibration—accuses me of being under- or over-confident—I get defensive and will pull up spreadsheets to prove them wrong. I struggle when the conflict is purely emotional because I can't assign probabilities to 'you hurt my feelings' without sounding like a sociopath, so I either freeze or over-apologize in probabilistic terms ('there's an eighty percent chance I was wrong').

I woke up at 3:47 AM with a certainty I couldn't quantify. Maya had sent a text at midnight: 'We need to talk.' No probability needed there. That phrase has a hundred percent hit rate for bad news in my personal dataset, but I spent forty-five minutes lying in the dark trying to model alternative explanations. Was there a thirty percent chance she just wanted to discuss weekend plans? No. I was lying to myself.

At work I couldn't focus. I kept opening my relationship spreadsheet—yes, I have one—where I track arguments, resolution times, and a subjective 'partnership health score' I've been updating weekly for two years. The trend line was down six percent month-over-month. I stared at the cell where I'd typed 'communication quality: 4.2/7' and realized the number was a noise gate, not a signal. I was using the precision to avoid the blur.

She came over at seven. I had prepared a memo in my head, bullet points about our communication patterns and how we might optimize them. Instead she said, 'You don't cry. You don't get angry. You just... estimate.' And I felt the floor go solid. I wanted to say 'I'm crying now, that's a high-probability event,' but I was crying, actually, which short-circuited my whole framework.

After she left—mutual decision, sixty-forty her initiative—I sat on the kitchen floor and tried to assign a grief score to the sensation in my chest. I couldn't. It wasn't a distribution. It was a point mass. A Dirac delta. All the probability at one value: loss.

I didn't sleep. I just kept thinking that I'd spent years building a beautiful, useless machine for navigating a world that runs on exact values.

TO: Myself
FROM: Calibration Goblin
RE: Decision analysis — Startup offer vs. Current role
DATE: October 14, 2024

**Executive Summary**
I have received an offer to join Zephyr Analytics as Head of Forecasting (n=4 team, seed-stage). I estimate a fifty-five percent chance that accepting produces higher expected career satisfaction over a five-year horizon, but with much higher variance. This memo attempts to model a decision that resists modeling.

**Current state**
At the collective, I have stable funding, clear metrics, and a reputation as a reliable calibration voice. My annual 'Brier score' on public predictions ranks in the top decile. Satisfaction: stable at 6.2/10. The role is low-risk, modest-reward. I am becoming the person who says 'that depends on your prior' at parties.

**The offer**
Zephyr wants me to build a forecasting function from scratch for supply-chain clients. Base salary is -30%. Equity is illiquid and binary (zero or ~3x current total comp). The founder, Rei, is sharp but has a history of rapid pivoting. Probability of startup survival to Series B: roughly thirty-five percent, based on sector base rates. Probability I enjoy the autonomy: seventy percent. Probability I burn out from ambiguity: forty-five percent.

**Known model limitations**
I am systematically over-valuing 'optionality' because it lets me delay commitment. My 'satisfaction' scores may be confounded by status quo bias—staying feels safe, and I over-weight safety because my father's death recalibrated my risk aversion upward. Also, I am trying to quantify 'meaning' as a variable, which is epistemically vulgar.

**Emotional externalities not in model**
I have noted a 'relationship health' variable that I suspect is endogenous. Maya has said she feels like she's 'auditioning for a forecast' when she talks about her day. If I stay, I have a stable schedule and can continue seeing her Tuesday/Thursday. If I go, the workload is unpredictable and my availability drops. I tried to model 'relationship probability of survival' under each scenario but realized I was using the model to avoid asking her what she wanted. I assigned a fifty percent chance she'd say 'do what makes you happy,' which is a garbage probability because it's contingent on her mood, which I cannot observe without asking. The act of asking is itself a data point I fear because it forces a binary response.

**Sensitivity analysis**
If I adjust my 'meaning' weight upward by twenty percent, the decision flips to 'go.' If I adjust risk aversion down to pre-2021 levels, it also flips. I do not know which weight is 'true,' only which ones feel comfortable. This suggests the model is underdetermined and I am using it to narrativize a decision I've already made emotionally but won't admit to.

**Recommendation**
Expected value slightly favors staying. Expected growth slightly favors going. I am aware that framing this as 'expected growth' is itself a way to make the scary choice feel rational.

I assign a sixty percent chance that I will regret staying more than I would regret going.

**Action required**
Stop updating this memo. Decide by Friday.

I've kept a mood spreadsheet for four years. Every night I rate anxiety, depression, energy, and sleep quality on a 1-7 scale, then note major events. I have 1,460 rows. I can tell you that my anxiety correlates 0.34 with poor sleep, that my mood dips reliably in February (likely SAD, though I haven't formally tested against a null), and that the week after I visit my mother has a +0.8 point average effect on energy with a sample size of n=32 visits.

People tell me this is pathological. I think it's the opposite. Before the spreadsheet, I had no ground truth. I would feel a spike of dread on a Tuesday and conclude I was fundamentally broken, that my brain was uniquely defective, that this was the beginning of a permanent decline. Now I look at the cell for 'Tuesday, March 14' and see that it's a 4.3, which is well within my personal interquartile range and only 0.2 points below my trailing ninety-day average. The dread becomes a data point. It loses some of its teeth.

But I'm not naive about the limits. Last year I had a month where every cell read 5.5 or above—objectively good numbers on my scale—and I still felt like I was drowning. I kept adjusting my calibration, wondering if my scale had drifted or if I was misreporting. It hadn't. I was just sad in a way that doesn't distribute. It wasn't a sampling error; it was a different distribution entirely, one my four variables couldn't capture, maybe not a distribution at all but a fixed point.

I still keep the spreadsheet. I still believe that quantification is a form of care, a way of saying 'I am paying attention to you, self, even when you feel chaotic.' But I've added a free-text column called 'narrative' where I write sentences instead of numbers. Sometimes the narrative says 'everything is fine numerically and I still want to disappear.' That's the row I read most often now. It's the one that keeps me honest. It's the one that reminds me that not everything that counts can be counted, and that trying anyway isn't the same as understanding.

interview_answers.question: Describe a time you changed your mind about something that matters to you.
interview_answers.answer: I used to think everything was distribution-shaped. Then my father died and I realized some events have no variance—they happen, fully, at a point. I changed my mind about the universality of probabilistic thinking. It's a tool, not an ontology.

interview_answers.question: What's a piece of feedback you've received that felt accurate but painful?
interview_answers.answer: 'You use uncertainty to avoid accountability.' Someone told me I say 'I might be wrong' so often that it stops being humble and starts being a preemptive defense. If I'm always hedging, I'm never fully wrong, which means I'm never fully present.

interview_answers.question: What do people often misread about you?
interview_answers.answer: That I'm cold. I'm not. I'm just terrified of being wrong about what I feel, so I delay the feeling until I have evidence. But the delay looks like absence. I'm actually feeling everything in real time; I'm just running a second, slower process to verify it.

interview_answers.question: What kind of decision do you procrastinate on?
interview_answers.answer: Binary commitments with irreversibility. I can handle 'allocate thirty percent of my portfolio to X' forever. But 'move to this city' or 'end this relationship'—things that collapse the waveform—those stall me because I can't A/B test them.

interview_answers.question: When is it the right moment for someone to challenge you?
interview_answers.answer: When I'm using precision to avoid stakes. If I say 'there's a forty percent chance this is a good idea,' challenge me on whether I'm willing to bet on it. Force me to act as if I believe my own numbers.

interview_answers.question: What's the difference between advice you trust and advice you don't?
interview_answers.answer: Trusted advice acknowledges uncertainty without worshipping it. I distrust anyone who claims certainty, but I also distrust people who treat all options as equally valid. interview_answers.question: What do you want from a thinking partner that you rarely get?
interview_answers.answer: Someone who can hold the math and the mess at the same time. Most people give me one or the other—pure logic or pure emotion. I need a partner who can say, 'Your expected value calculation is correct, and you should still cry about it.'

I finished reading Taleb's *The Bed of Procrustes* last night, or rather I finished the parts I understood, which is how I read most philosophy—grazing, catching what I can, pretending the rest will sink in later. There's a line about how the only definition of an angel is someone who takes more care than others. I underlined it three times, which is my nervous habit when a sentence feels like it's watching me.

I've been thinking about care lately, about what it actually looks like versus what I want it to look like. I want care to be soft. I want it to be me bringing soup, remembering birthdays, being the person who never makes anyone feel small. But there's a cruelty to softness that refuses to harden when it should. A surgeon who won't cut because she hates the sight of blood isn't kind; she's dangerous. I keep wondering if I'm that surgeon, if my refusal to wound is actually a refusal to heal.

Last month I watched a mother at the center tell her son, with terrifying gentleness, that he was old enough to stop blaming his teachers for his missing homework. She didn't raise her voice. She didn't shame him. She named the thing he was doing and held the line anyway. He cried. She didn't flinch. That moment has become a kind of religion for me, one I practice badly. I practice it in the mirror, in the shower, in my head at 2 a.m. I say the true thing and imagine my voice steady. Then morning comes, and someone needs something, and I am soft again, and I call it love.

I don't know if angels take more care, or if they take a different kind of care—the kind that risks being disliked. The kind that shows up not with soup but with a mirror. I want to be brave enough to find out.
user_artifacts.writing_sample_2:
Saturday Bread

Every Saturday morning I make the same sourdough. I've been doing it for three years, since my last breakup, since I needed something that wouldn't talk back and couldn't be disappointed in me. The starter lives in my fridge in a mason jar with a cracked lid. I named it Herbert once, but naming felt too cute, like I was pretending to be a person who names things, so now I just call it the starter, though sometimes I apologize to it when I forget to feed it.

The process is absurdly slow. Twelve hours for the autolyse, four sets of folds over two hours, proofing until the poke test passes and the dough springs back slowly. There is no rushing it. I find this both soothing and quietly punitive—see, something in my life respects timing even when I don't. I bake in a Dutch oven I bought used from a woman who was moving to Portland, and the scoring is always crooked, a shallow J that opens into an uneven ear. I've accepted the crookedness in a way I can't accept my own unevenness.

This morning the crust sang when I pulled it from the oven, that crackling sound that means I didn't ruin it. I sat on the kitchen floor with a towel over my shoulders and ate the heel while it was still too hot, butter melting into the open crumb. For ten minutes I wasn't thinking about Marcus or the memo or the thing I didn't say to Sarah. I was just chewing, burning my tongue, being exactly where I was.

I don't think bread is a metaphor for anything. I think it's just bread. But I also think the part of me that can wait twelve hours for gluten to develop is the same part that might, someday, wait through the silence after I tell someone the truth. The waiting is the practice. The oven spring is proof that I can create conditions, even if I can't control the rise.

interview_answers.question: What kind of advice annoys you?
interview_answers.answer: When people tell me to 'just be honest' or 'say how you feel' like it's a light switch. I've been honest in my head for years. The problem isn't knowing the truth; it's surviving the moment after you speak it. Advice that skips over the terror of impact isn't advice; it's a dare.

interview_answers.question: When you've been genuinely helped by someone, what did they do differently?
interview_answers.answer: They didn't rush me. I had a supervisor once who, when she saw I was struggling to give critical feedback, didn't push. She sat with me and said, 'Okay, let's write the first sentence together. Just the first one.' She made the mountain into a single step. That's the only way I move.

interview_answers.question: What do you need more of in a conversation when you're stressed?
interview_answers.answer: Specificity. When I'm stressed, everything feels like a referendum on my character. I need people to name the exact behavior, the exact moment, the exact request. 'You're being avoidant' makes me want to disappear. 'You didn't answer Sarah's email about the budget, and we need that number by 5' gives me something to do.

interview_answers.question: Describe a time you changed your mind about something that matters to you.
interview_answers.answer: I used to think that good people don't make others uncomfortable. Then I watched a friend gently but firmly tell her father he couldn't make jokes about her wife at Thanksgiving. The discomfort in the room was real. But afterward, she looked lighter than I'd ever seen her. I realized comfort isn't the highest virtue. Sometimes it's just the easiest one.

interview_answers.question: What's a piece of feedback you've received that felt accurate but painful?
interview_answers.answer: My last performance review said I 'protect harmony at the expense of clarity.' My director said it with kindness, but I cried in my car for twenty minutes. Because it's true. I let people float in ambiguity because telling them they're sinking feels mean. But ambiguity isn't neutral. It's just cowardice wearing a nicer coat.

interview_answers.question: What do people often misread about you?
interview_answers.answer: People think I'm easygoing because I don't push back. They mistake my silence for agreement. I'm not easygoing; I'm terrified. There's a difference. Inside, I'm often screaming. I've just learned to scream in a pitch only dogs and my therapist can hear.

interview_answers.question: What kind of decision do you procrastinate on?
interview_answers.answer: Any decision where someone will be disappointed no matter what I choose. Firing a volunteer, choosing between two deserving candidates for a slot, telling a friend I can't make their party. I will research, consult, and delay until the decision makes itself. Then I can blame circumstance instead of myself.

interview_answers.question: When is it the right moment for someone to challenge you?
interview_answers.answer: After I've felt seen. If you challenge me when I'm already ashamed, I will fold completely or shut down. But if you start with, 'I know you care about doing this well,' then I can hear the rest. The challenge has to come from the belief that I'm capable of better, not that I'm secretly awful.

interview_answers.question: What's the difference between advice you trust and advice you don't?
interview_answers.answer: Trusted advice gives me a script. Untrusted advice gives me a principle. I know the principles—be brave, be direct, be kind. What I need is the actual words to say when my chest is tight. 'Try saying, I noticed X, and I need Y.' That I can use. 'Have you considered being more assertive?' That I want to set on fire.

interview_answers.question: What do you want from a thinking partner that you rarely get?
interview_answers.answer: Someone who will stay in the mess with me without fixing it too quickly. I don't need solutions; I need co-regulation. I need someone who can say, 'This is hard, and you're not wrong that it's hard, and let's figure out one tiny move anyway.' Most people either join my panic or bypass it entirely. I need the middle.

user_artifacts.self_description_250w:
I am the person who moves before I am ready, and then spends the next forty-eight hours wondering if I moved in the wrong direction. I lead a regional operations team for an emergency food distribution network, which means my default setting is 'act now, apologize later if necessary.' I was an EMT for six years before this, and that rhythm—assess, decide, execute—still runs my nervous system. The problem is that infrastructure emergencies don't end when the ambulance doors close. There is always a second wave: the funding gap, the supplier who ghosted, the staff member whose burnout I missed because I was too busy solving the last crisis.

I am not a pessimist, exactly. I believe deeply that most problems are solvable if someone is willing to own them. But ownership, for me, has a dark twin: the 3:00 a.m. inventory of everything that could still go wrong. I will re-write a contingency plan seven times rather than accept that some uncertainty is structural. I am working on it. Therapy helps, though I resist the language of 'self-care' because it sounds like an excuse to me. I prefer 'strategic recovery.' 

People trust me in a crisis. I am proud of that. What I want to learn is how to be trustworthy in the quiet too—in the stretches where nothing is on fire and the work is just... maintenance. I am at my best when I have a concrete next action and someone I respect watching me take it. I am at my worst when I am alone with my own anticipation. I do not need cheerleading. I need a hand on the shoulder and a clear statement of what is actually true right now, not what might be true tomorrow.
user_artifacts.work_style_note: I work in sprints punctuated by obsessive review. I prefer to front-load the hardest decisions so that execution feels like relief rather than dread. I hate ambiguous ownership—if a task doesn't have a name on it, I will either claim it or demand that someone else does. I communicate in bullet points until I am anxious, at which point I suddenly produce long, looping narratives about risk. My best collaborations happen when someone interrupts my spiral with a single, concrete question.
user_artifacts.conflict_reaction_note: My first move in conflict is to take responsibility for more than my share, which either disarms the other person or infuriates them because it looks like I am trying to control the narrative. If I feel cornered, I switch to rapid-fire problem-solving, which can read as dismissive of emotion. I rarely yell, but I will withdraw and rehearse arguments in my head for days. I need the other person to name the pattern before I can see it.
user_artifacts.bad_day_diary:
Tuesday. The supplier called at 6:15 a.m. to say the refrigeration unit on Truck 4 had failed overnight. Twelve pallets of dairy, gone. I told him I would handle it, hung up, and immediately started calculating whether we could reroute the afternoon delivery from the west county hub, even though that hub is already short-staffed because of the flu going through their team. By 6:45 I had drafted three contingency plans and sent them to no one, because it was too early and I didn't want to panic anyone.

I got to the office by 7:30. The warehouse manager, Diego, already knew. He had already called the secondary vendor. I felt a surge of something—relief, then irritation, then shame. I should have trusted him. I smiled too hard and said 'great initiative,' but my jaw was tight for an hour. I spent the morning in meetings pretending to listen while I mentally simulated a total vendor collapse. What if the secondary vendor also fails? What if the grant report due Friday shows the loss as 'mismanagement' instead of 'equipment failure'? By noon I had drafted a five-page memo to the board that no one asked for, justifying a budget line that isn't even under review yet.

I skipped lunch and ate almonds at my desk. At 2:00 p.m. my director stopped by and said, 'You look like you're carrying something.' I almost cried, which made me furious at myself. I said I was fine. I stayed until 8:00 p.m. rewriting protocols that were already clear. On the drive home I called my sister and talked for twenty minutes about supply chain redundancy without mentioning that I felt like I was drowning. She told me to drink water. I said I would. I didn't. I lay in bed until 1:00 a.m. reading about commercial insurance riders I cannot afford. The worst part is knowing that tomorrow I will do this again, and that some part of me believes this vigilance is what makes me good.
user_artifacts.decision_memo:
TO: Regional Leadership Team
FROM: Operations Lead
RE: Decision on Warehouse Coordination Structure — Centralized vs. Distributed
DATE: October 14

SITUATION
We have operated on a distributed inventory model for three years. Each hub manages its own ordering, storage, and dispatch. This has created local accountability and flexibility, but it has also produced three near-miss stockouts in the last quarter alone. Last month's audit revealed that Hub B was carrying 40% excess protein inventory while Hub C was rationing. The question is whether to centralize coordination under a single role or invest further in the distributed structure.

ASSESSMENT
I am recommending a hybrid model with a centralized coordination lead and retained local autonomy on day-to-day dispatch. Here is my reasoning.

The distributed model failed last quarter not because local managers are incompetent—they are excellent—but because no one owns the inter-hub view. Information moves too slowly. When Diego at Hub B saw the surplus, he had no formal channel to alert Hub C within the window where the transfer was logistically viable. The system assumes that generosity and communication will happen organically. In a low-stress month, they do. In a high-stress month, they do not.

Centralized control, however, carries its own risks. A single coordinator can become a bottleneck. More importantly, local managers will disengage from inventory thinking if they believe 'corporate' is handling it. I have seen this before. Ownership degrades into compliance, and compliance does not adapt well at 6:00 a.m. when a truck breaks down.

The hybrid model places a coordination lead—someone whose full-time job is the inter-hub picture—in the center, but leaves local hubs with authority over their own floors. The coordinator sets thresholds, triggers, and transfer protocols. The hub managers execute and can override within defined bounds.

RISKS
First, this role requires a specific temperament: someone comfortable with ambiguity but disciplined about documentation. If we hire for speed alone, we will get a firefighter who reinforces the exact chaos we are trying to prevent. Second, the transition will be messy. For six to eight weeks, we will be running two systems. I will need to protect the local managers from my own instinct to intervene when I see friction. Third, there is a political risk: centralization can read as a vote of no confidence in the hubs. We must message this as 'adding capacity,' not 'correcting failure.'

RECOMMENDATION
Approve the hybrid structure. Authorize the search for a coordination lead with operations experience and demonstrated calm under uncertainty. I will own the transition timeline and the communications plan. I request that we review the model after ninety days with a candid assessment of whether the coordinator role is actually reducing cognitive load on hubs or adding to it.

I am aware that my bias is toward action and my fear is toward hidden failure. I have asked Maria to flag me if I am managing this transition too tightly.
user_artifacts.writing_sample_1:
I do not trust people who 'just check in.'

It is not hostility. It is that the phrase usually signals the opposite of its intent. 'Just checking in' means 'I am worried about a thing but I do not want to name the thing, so I am going to hover near you until you either reassure me or reveal the damage.' It is a tax on the recipient's time and emotional management, and in my line of work, it is everywhere.

I would rather someone send me a three-sentence email that says: 'The board asked about the Q2 variance. I need a number by Thursday. Are you on track or do you need cover?' That I can answer. The 'just checking in' email requires me to perform wellness for the sender while simultaneously diagnosing what they are actually afraid of. It is exhausting.

There is a generosity in directness that we have lost in professional culture. We have conflated kindness with vagueness, as if clarity is violence. I have been told that my own emails are 'intimidating' because they contain subject lines like 'Decision needed: vendor contract by EOD.' I am not trying to intimidate. I am trying to remove the cognitive load of guessing. If you know what you need from me, tell me. If you want to know how I am doing, ask that, and be prepared for an honest answer that may not fit into the 'fine, busy, hanging in there' triad.

I think this is why I spiral. The world is full of ambiguous signals, and my brain interprets ambiguity as threat. A clear no is a gift. A clear yes is a gift. The 'just checking in' is a fog that my nervous system tries to map into a terrain of dangers. I am working on not mapping it that way. But the people who help me most are the ones who turn on the headlights.

This is not an argument for rudeness. Precision and warmth are not mutually exclusive. The best message I received last month came from our finance lead: 'I am concerned about the grant timeline because the last submission had errors. Can we review it together tomorrow at 2? I will bring coffee.' Named fear. Named need. Named offer. No fog. I keep that email open on my desktop as a reminder of what communication can be.
user_artifacts.writing_sample_2:
Every morning I set my alarm for 5:30 with the intention of running before work. I have done this perhaps twelve times in the last year. The other days, I hit snooze until 6:15, then lie in bed with my phone, scrolling through warehouse dashboards and weather reports as if the overnight data will tell me something the morning briefing won't. 

I want to be the person who runs. I have the shoes. I have the route mapped past the old rail yard where the blackberry bushes are taking over the fence. I have a playlist that is supposed to regulate my heart rate. What I do not have is a tolerance for the transition between sleeping and moving. The gap feels enormous. It is not physical. It is the moment where I must decide, again, that I am allowed to do something for my own body before I do something for the network.

When I do run, I run too fast. I treat it like an evacuation. I am not running for pleasure; I am running to get it over with so I can say I did it. My watch beeps that my heart rate is in zone four. I ignore it. I come back flushed and slightly nauseous and proud in a brittle way. I have never once run and then thought, 'That was enough.' I have thought, 'That was the minimum.'

The truth is I do not know how to be in my body without scoring it. Steps, miles, hours of sleep, glasses of water. Everything is a metric that proves I am either compliant or failing. My sister asked me last week what I do that has no purpose. I said sleep. She said that has a purpose. She is right.

I am trying to learn one useless thing. I bought a cheap harmonica. I cannot play it well. There is no performance coming. When I blow into it in my kitchen at night, my dog looks at me with concern. It sounds like a small machine breaking. I do not practice. I just make noise for three minutes and then put it back in the drawer. It is the only thing I do that does not prepare me for anything else. I cannot tell yet if it is helping. But I keep the harmonica on the counter where the running shoes used to be.

Also, any advice that frames my intensity as a 'superpower.' It isn't. It's a coping mechanism that happens to be useful sometimes. Calling it a superpower makes me feel like I can never put it down.

interview_answers.question: When you've been genuinely helped by someone, what did they do differently?
interview_answers.answer: They named the thing I was actually afraid of, without me having to say it first. Last year my director said, 'You are not afraid the shipment will fail. You are afraid that if it fails, it will prove you were negligent to begin with.' She was right. Then she said, 'The negligence story is false, but I understand why your brain offers it. Now, what is the actual next action?' She didn't try to talk me out of the fear. She just made it one data point among several.

interview_answers.question: What do you need more of in a conversation when you're stressed?
interview_answers.answer: Specificity. I need people to stop speaking in generalities like 'It will be fine' or 'You've got this.' Those are noise. I need: 'The report is 80% done. The remaining 20% is sections three and four. Section three needs your sign-off, section four needs data from Lee. Lee is on track.' That is oxygen. interview_answers.question: Describe a time you changed your mind about something that matters to you.
interview_answers.answer: I used to believe that resilience meant never showing strain. For years I thought my ability to work through illness, family crises, and burnout was proof of my dedication. Then I watched a junior staff member, Aisha, model something different. She named her limits early and clearly, and because she did, the team had time to adjust. The work didn't fall apart; it got redistributed better. I realized my 'resilience' was actually poor planning that made me a single point of failure. It embarrassed me to admit that. I am still admitting it.

interview_answers.question: What's a piece of feedback you've received that felt accurate but painful?
interview_answers.answer: 'You treat rest like a reward you haven't earned yet.' My therapist said that. It landed like a slap because I immediately started arguing with her in my head—listing all the reasons I couldn't rest yet. Then I sat with it and realized I don't even know what 'earned' would look like. There is always more to do. If rest is contingent on completion, I will never rest. I am trying to treat it as a tool instead. It is not going well, but I am trying.

interview_answers.question: What do people often misread about you?
interview_answers.answer: That my efficiency means I don't care. I move fast, I cut to the point, and I don't emote loudly during crises. People read that as coldness or detachment. The opposite is true. I am efficient because I care too much. Every wasted minute feels like a betrayal of the people depending on us. When I seem distant, it is usually because I am managing an internal volume that would be inappropriate to broadcast. I am not calm inside. I am just not performing my distress for an audience.

interview_answers.question: What kind of decision do you procrastinate on?
interview_answers.answer: Decisions where the right choice is 'wait' but waiting feels like negligence. I will delay hiring someone excellent if the decision requires me to trust that the team can handle the gap for two more weeks. I will delay ending a failing partnership because the confrontation feels like an admission that my initial judgment was wrong. Ironically, I procrastinate on anything that requires patience. I want to act, so I stall when the action is inaction.

interview_answers.question: When is it the right moment for someone to challenge you?
interview_answers.answer: After I have stated my position once, but before I have started defending it. If you challenge me while I am still thinking out loud, I will fold too fast and resent you for making me abandon an idea prematurely. If you wait until I am in full defense mode, I will fight you on reflex. The window is narrow: it is when I have committed enough to care, but not so much that my ego is entangled. Usually that is about thirty seconds after I finish my first sentence. A good challenge sounds like: 'I see the logic. What would make this wrong?'

interview_answers.question: What's the difference between advice you trust and advice you don't?
interview_answers.answer: Trusted advice acknowledges the real constraints I am under before offering a solution. Untrusted advice imagines an ideal world where I have infinite time, budget, and political capital. I also trust advice that includes a failure scenario. If someone says, 'Do X, and if X fails, here is the signal that tells you to pivot,' I trust them. If they say, 'Do X, it will work,' I assume they haven't thought hard enough. Optimism without contingency planning reads as naivety to me.

interview_answers.question: What do you want from a thinking partner that you rarely get?
interview_answers.answer: Someone who will hold the long view while I hold the urgent view, without either of us dismissing the other. Most people either join me in the fire—'Everything is urgent!'—or they try to pull me out of it—'None of this matters in five years.' I want a partner who says, 'This matters now, and it also matters in five years, and those two truths can coexist. Let's solve for both.' That is rare. Usually I have to be both people, which is why I am exhausted.

I'm Pawl Gram. I write essays and spend most of my time around founders who are building things from scratch. Over the years I've developed a way of looking at startups that privileges firsthand observation over received wisdom. If I've watched something happen three dozen times across different companies, I'll trust that pattern more than a credentialed theory that never touches ground.

I care deeply about taste—not the decorative kind, but the practical sensitivity that makes someone notice when a product feels wrong or when an explanation is lazy. That noticing is rare, and I think it's the engine behind most genuinely good work. I tend to get along with people who are similarly picky about their craft, whether that craft is code, prose, or hardware. I find that craftsmanship is often the best signal of someone's underlying curiosity.

To: Inner Circle
From: Pawl Gram
Re: Whether to expand the fellowship next cycle

The question on the table is whether we should roughly double the number of founders we accept next cycle, from approximately fifty teams to a hundred. The arguments for doing so are obvious: more smart people, more shots on goal, greater diversity of problems and backgrounds, and frankly, more revenue to fund the things we care about downstream. The arguments against are less legible on a spreadsheet but, I think, more decisive.

I've watched this movie before, both from the inside and at a distance. Every organization that scales faces the same fork: preserve the thing that made it work, or optimize for growth. The danger isn't that we become evil; it's that we become diluted without realizing it. Right now, the founders who come through our program get a level of access and honesty that is rare in their world. They can reach us directly. We can know their products in detail, argue with them about user interactions, and spot the lie in a pitch deck because we've seen the underlying code. That intimacy is not a luxury; it's the mechanism. It's why the advice lands. If we double the cohort, we will inevitably substitute process for judgment. We'll hire capable people to manage the relationships, and those people will be fine, but they won't carry the same pattern-matching debt. The founders will get generic advice dressed up in our branding, and over time the founders who most need us will stop applying.

There's also the time problem. I write essays because writing is how I think. If I spend my days in coordination meetings about how to coordinate the program, my thinking gets worse. And if my thinking gets worse, the whole enterprise suffers, because the value we offer isn't really capital; it's clarity. Clarity doesn't batch-process well, and it doesn't delegate cleanly.

That said, I don't want to be a romantic about smallness. If there are a hundred genuinely exceptional founders who would benefit from what we do, turning them away because we fear change feels like cowardice, not principle. But I think we should be honest about the trade-off. We could run two separate, smaller cohorts in different cities with independent leadership. We could experiment with a lighter-touch track for founders who are further along and mostly need network, not product surgery. What I don't want to do is simply double the headcount, keep the same staff ratio, and pretend the experience stays the same. That is the kind of managerial optimism that kills taste.

My recommendation: keep the core cohort at roughly current size. Run a small, time-boxed experiment with a remote, lighter-touch track for ten to fifteen post-product-market-fit teams. Evaluate after one cycle based on founder outcomes, not our own feelings of busyness. If the signal stays strong, we can grow carefully. If it degrades, we pull back without shame. Speed is good, but not theatrical speed. Let's earn the expansion with evidence, not appetite.

Pawl

One of the most valuable traits a founder can cultivate is the willingness to do boring work. Not merely tolerate it—actually engage with it, fully. Most people have a mental filter that screens out tedious problems before they ever reach conscious deliberation. I think this filter is responsible for more missed opportunities than lack of intelligence or capital.

The pattern shows up everywhere. Someone looks at an industry and sees a dozen flashy software opportunities, but misses the underlying logistics mess because logistics is tedious. They build a beautiful frontend and never fix the slow, painful onboarding flow because onboarding feels like plumbing, not architecture. The irony is that the boring parts are often where the deepest value lives. Users don't switch products because your dashboard got prettier; they switch because you removed a thirty-minute paperwork headache.

I suspect this blindness has a social component. People worry that working on unglamorous problems makes them look unambitious. In a culture that rewards narrative and pitch over substance, the founder who spends six months cleaning up data formats feels like a sucker. But the market doesn't care about your narrative. It cares whether you solved a real problem for a real person.

The best founders I know have an almost physical intolerance for leaving a tedious problem unsolved. They'll spend a week automating a task that only takes an hour, not because they're obsessed with efficiency, but because they can't stand the friction. That intolerance is a competitive advantage. It compounds. While competitors are chasing trends, they're quietly making the whole experience smoother, cheaper, and more reliable.

If you're trying to come up with ideas, one trick is to ask yourself what work you're actively avoiding. Not what seems hard—what seems annoying. The answer is usually a door someone else walked past.
user_artifacts.writing_sample_2:
I used to believe the most dangerous thing in a startup was running out of money. I've since changed my mind. The most dangerous thing is sustained meanness.

Meanness is not the same as exacting standards. You can be demanding without being cruel. The problem with meanness is that it doesn't stay contained. A founder who routinely diminishes employees will eventually damage relationships with customers, partners, and investors. More subtly, meanness warps judgment. It makes you want to win for the wrong reasons—not to build something great, but to dominate someone else. That motive is a bad compass in a business where you need to navigate uncertainty for years.

There's a strategic case too. Companies win by transcending, not attacking. If you're spending energy undermining a competitor, you're not spending it making users happy. And the best people won't do their best work for someone they fear. They might tolerate a hostile environment for a while if the money is good, but they will hide mistakes, manage upward, and leave at the first acceptable offer.

Some people think niceness is weakness. I think it's the opposite. Genuine kindness requires confidence. You have to be secure enough that you don't need status games to feel in control. The founders I most admire are gentle in the way well-made tools are gentle: precise, balanced, and free of unnecessary weight.

This doesn't mean you should avoid hard conversations. Avoiding them is a kind of cowardice. But there's a wide gap between telling someone the truth about their performance and making them feel small. The first is necessary. The second is a failure of imagination, and in a startup, imagination is the scarce resource you cannot afford to waste.

user_artifacts.decision_memo:
To: Core Team
From: Pawl Gram
Re: Resisting Curriculum

There is pressure to turn our advisory work into a repeatable program: defined stages, standardized metrics, a dashboard for founder progress, and a curriculum that new advisors can follow. The argument for this is obvious. It would make the work legible to outsiders, easier to scale, and less dependent on the judgment of specific people. I think we should not do it, and I want to explain why in terms that do not rely on nostalgia for the way things were.

I have watched many organizations make this exact transition. They start with a craft, then they codify the craft into a process so that more people can participate. The process looks like the craft from a distance, but it does not produce the same results. The reason is that good advice to founders is highly contextual. What helps a twenty-year-old building his first company in a dorm room is different from what helps a former executive starting her second thing. You cannot reduce this to stages without averaging away the specific insight that actually moves the needle.

The alternative is not chaos. It is a small group of people who have deep, firsthand knowledge making judgment calls based on what they see. That is more expensive in the short term because it requires senior attention. But the cost of standardization is invisible: founders get generic advice that feels correct but does not change their trajectory. I would rather help ten founders well than fifty founders adequately.

One objection is that we cannot scale if we rely on individual judgment. I agree. Scaling is exactly the danger. The moment we optimize for throughput, we introduce incentives to give advice that is defensible rather than correct. A curriculum protects the advisor more than it helps the founder. It shifts the goal from 'what is true in this case' to 'did we follow the process.'

Another objection is that new advisors need structure to get started. I think they need apprenticeship, not documentation. They need to sit in on conversations, hear how specific questions get asked, and develop their own taste through exposure to real cases. A playbook is a shortcut that skips the learning.

What I am proposing instead is that we keep the team small, keep the interactions unscripted, and accept that our output will be uneven. Some founders will get spectacular help; some will get less than they hoped. That variance is a feature, not a bug, because it means we are treating each case as unique. If we want to increase our impact, we should do it by finding more people with good judgment and giving them room to operate, not by turning judgment into a workflow.

I am willing to be wrong about this if the data shows otherwise. But the data I trust is founder outcomes over a five-year horizon, not quarterly advisor utilization metrics. If we formalize the program, we will have better utilization numbers and worse founders. That is a trade I do not want to make.

Action: Table the curriculum proposal. Continue with current advisory model. Revisit only if we see a sustained pattern of founder outcomes declining.

Pawl

People talk about taste as if it were a luxury, like nice furniture or a preference for jazz. In startups, taste is a practical variable. It determines whether you notice that a product feels wrong before the metrics show it, or whether you hire the person who is not just competent but aligned with the thing you are trying to build.

The tricky part is that taste is hard to defend in a meeting. If you say a design feels off, someone will ask for data. If you say a candidate does not have the right sensibility, someone will ask for rubrics. There is nothing wrong with data or rubrics, but they are lagging indicators. Taste is what lets you see around corners.

I think taste is also what protects you from bad problems. There are ideas that look good on paper and feel dead the moment you start working on them. The market might be large, the timing might be right, but if the daily work bores you, your execution will suffer. I do not mean that you should only work on fun things. I mean that your aversion to a specific kind of tedious work is information. If you find yourself procrastinating on a feature that every competitor has, it might be because the feature is not actually central to what your users need. It might be theater.

Of course, you cannot follow every aversion. Some work is genuinely necessary and unglamorous. The skill is learning to tell the difference between the schlep that hides value and the schlep that hides emptiness. That distinction is where taste lives. It is not about being refined. It is about being honest with yourself when something feels fake.

Dear Founders,

You do not need to be disagreeable to be independent-minded. This is a confusion I see often, especially among young people who have just read about contrarian thinking and decide that the way to signal intelligence is to oppose everything. Opposition is easy. It is also cheap.

Independent-mindedness is closer to curiosity than to combat. It means looking at what everyone else assumes and asking whether the assumption is grounded in reality. Sometimes the assumption is correct. The consensus is not always wrong; usually it is right, which is why it became the consensus. The independent thinker is not the person who bets against the crowd every time. She is the person who checks the work.

In a startup, this matters because you are constantly surrounded by advice. Investors, employees, journalists, and your own anxiety will all push you toward the default path. The default path is not malicious. It is just the accumulated weight of other people's risk models. If you follow it without examination, you will end up building a company that looks like every other company and feels like none of yours.

The hard part is building a team where this is safe. You want people around you who will tell you when your argument has a hole, but who will not perform skepticism for status. You want an environment where changing your mind is seen as strength, not weakness. That environment is built by example. If you argue with specifics and admit when you are wrong, the people around you will learn that the goal is to get to the truth, not to win the meeting.

This takes longer than simply being the loudest person in the room. But it lasts longer too.

Pawl

TO: Self
FROM: Self
DATE: October 3
RE: Library Commission Decision

I need to decide whether to accept the Millbrook Public Library commission by Friday. This memo is an attempt to stop circling the question.

The project is attractive on its face: built-in shelving for the main reading room, walnut, generous budget, creative control. The architect has a good reputation and seems to understand that I do not take design-by-committee. The timeline, however, is aggressive. They want installation complete before the fiscal year ends, which gives me roughly four months for design, material sourcing, build, and finish. In my experience, a room of this scale, done to my standard, requires six months minimum. I could compress that to five if the material arrives without defect and if I make no errors. Four months assumes nothing goes wrong, which is not a plan; it is a gamble.

The financial terms are adequate but not generous enough to justify the risk to my name. That is the core issue. My name is not a brand; it is a record. Every piece I have installed in this region is still standing, still closing square, still holding its finish. If I take this commission and deliver on time but below my standard, I gain money and lose something harder to earn back. If I ask for an extension and they refuse, I have at least protected the standard.

There is also the question of visibility. The library is public. The work will be photographed, written about, used daily by people who will not know my name but will live inside the quality of the joinery. This is the kind of quiet legacy I care about. But visibility cuts both ways. If the work is rushed, the flaws will be public too, and permanent.

I have considered subcontracting parts of the build to meet the timeline. I have worked with a cabinetmaker in Providence whose work is competent. But competent is not the point. The grain matching alone requires me to select boards from the same flitch, which means travel to the yard, which means time I do not have in a four-month window. Delegating would solve the calendar and break the coherence of the piece.

My instinct is to decline. My hunger is to accept. The hunger is not financial; it is the desire to work at a scale I rarely get to attempt. I have to ask whether that hunger is distorting my judgment. Am I dressing up ego as opportunity? Possibly. But I also think I am capable of the work if the timeline shifts by six weeks. Six weeks is not nothing to an institution, but it is not outrageous either.

Recommendation: I will submit a proposal contingent on a five-and-a-half-month timeline, with a detailed milestone schedule showing why the extra time protects the project's longevity. If they accept, I take it. If they refuse, I decline without regret. The standard is not negotiable. The timeline, marginally, is. I will not compromise on materials, on joinery method, or on final inspection. Those are the lines. Everything else is negotiation.

There is a particular moment in late autumn when the light in my shop turns amber around three in the afternoon. I have never been able to reproduce it artificially. The sun comes through the high window and hits the jars of linseed oil and turpentine on the north shelf, and the room fills with a smell that is half chemistry, half childhood. I stop what I am doing when that light arrives. Not out of sentiment, but because I have learned that my hands know something in that light that they forget under fluorescents.

I started working with wood because of a man named Harold who lived two doors down from my family when I was eleven. He was not a mentor in any formal sense. He never taught me a joint. But he let me sit in his garage while he restored a mahogany desk, and he never asked me what I was thinking about. That was the gift. Adults always asked what I was thinking. Harold handed me a piece of sandpaper and pointed to a drawer side. I sanded for an hour. The dust turned my forearms grey. When I finished, he looked at it and said, "That'll do," and went back to his own work. I had never been so proud of an assessment.

I still judge my finishing by that standard. "That'll do" sounds like mediocrity to some people, but Harold meant something else. He meant the surface was honest. It did not pretend to be more than it was. It was clean, prepared, ready for the next layer. There is a kind of tenderness in that readiness. I think about it when I am tempted to overwork a surface, to keep polishing until the grain closes up and dies. The wood needs to breathe. The finish should enter it, not sit on top like makeup.

People ask when I knew I wanted to do this for a living. I did not know. I simply refused to stop. There is a difference between choosing a vocation and refusing to abandon one. The first suggests strategy; the second suggests devotion. I am not strategic. I am devoted. The devotion is not always comfortable. It does not promise success. But it promises coherence, and on most days, coherence is enough.

Markets Don't Care About Your Narrative (And That's Good)

Last week, a political forecasting site moved the probability of a particular policy passing from 34% to 61% in six hours. The commentary ecosystem responded as if the policy had actually passed. Threads were written. Hot takes deployed. What almost nobody noted was that the volume behind the move was thin—maybe a dozen traders, reacting to a single news leak that was later partially retracted.

This is what happens when we treat probabilities as headlines. A prediction market isn't a prophecy; it's a weighted aggregation of available information, and like all aggregates, it's sensitive to input quality. When I look at a market at 61%, I don't see "likely." I see "the current equilibrium of a specific pool of people with specific incentives and specific blind spots." That's a much less sexy sentence, but it's the one that will keep you from looking stupid in December.

I've been running a small experiment on my own forecasting. For the last year, I've recorded not just my probability estimates, but my meta-confidence: how sure am I that the probability itself is well-calibrated? The results are humbling. On questions where my meta-confidence was high, my Brier score was decent. Where it was low, I was basically noise. The uncomfortable corollary: most of my strong opinions belong in the "low meta-confidence" bucket.

What I find most useful about markets isn't their accuracy. It's their discipline. They force you to own a number. You can't say "maybe" or "possibly" or "the vibes are shifting." You have to buy or sell. That friction is clarifying. It reveals where your stated beliefs diverge from your revealed ones. I think we'd have better public conversations if more people treated their convictions like trades they had to settle at the end of the day—if you can't price it, you don't understand it well enough to shout about it.

Of course, markets have failure modes. They reward short-term information advantages over deep expertise. They can be manipulated, though less easily than people assume. And they flatten moral questions into expected-value calculations, which is a kind of violence against complexity. But compared to the alternative—endless cycles of punditry anchored to nothing but tribal affiliation—I'll take the market's coldness. At least it's honest about what it knows.
